c: Look before you measure

Start with your eyes and nose, with the power off. Look for a part in backwards, a wire in the wrong hole, a solder bridge between two pins, a joint that never flowed, a component missing entirely. Look for scorch marks, bulging capacitors and cracked parts. Smell for the sharp odour of burnt electronics. Compare the build against the schematic, one connection at a time. A large share of faults are found at this stage without any instrument.
Power first, always

If nothing obvious appears, apply power and measure the supply. Is the voltage present at the input? Is it present after the regulator, and is it the right value? Is it present at the power pin of every chip, measured at the pin itself and not at the supply? Is ground really connected everywhere? Experienced technicians check power first every time, because a missing or sagging supply produces symptoms that look like a dozen other faults.
Feel for heat

With the circuit powered, carefully check for anything getting hot. A chip or regulator that is too hot to keep a finger on is usually being asked for too much current, often because of a short downstream or a part fitted backwards. Use the back of a finger and be cautious, since a shorted part can burn. A part that should be warm and is stone cold is also information: it may not be getting power at all.
Split the circuit in half

For a circuit with several stages, do not check them in order. Check the middle. If the signal is correct at the midpoint, the fault lies in the second half. If not, it is in the first. Then split the faulty half again. This approach finds a fault in a chain of sixteen stages in four measurements. It is the same strategy as looking up a word in a dictionary by opening it in the middle.
Know what you expect

A measurement is only useful if you have a prediction to compare it with. Before touching the probe to a point, decide what the voltage should be there and why. If the reading matches, move on. If it does not, you have found something. People who probe without expectations collect numbers and learn nothing. Working out what each point ought to read is also how you come to understand the circuit properly.
Change one thing at a time

When you think you have found the cause, make one change and test. If you change three things and the circuit starts working, you do not know which mattered, and if it gets worse, you do not know which to undo. Keep notes of what you measured and what you changed. Twenty minutes into a difficult fault, it is easy to forget which combinations have been tried, and you start repeating yourself.
Suspect your assumptions

The hardest faults are the ones where something you were sure about is wrong. The new part is faulty. The wire you trust is broken inside its insulation. The chip is a different version with a different pinout. The supply is fine at rest and collapses under load. When nothing makes sense, list what you have assumed without checking and test each item. Explaining the problem aloud to someone else, or to nobody, often exposes the hidden assumption.
The usual suspects

Faults cluster. In new builds: wiring errors, reversed parts, bad solder joints, missing ground connections and wrong values. In old equipment: dried-out capacitors, cracked solder joints near connectors and anything that gets hot, corroded contacts and worn switches. In anything with a microcontroller: the code. Before concluding that you have found a rare and interesting failure, rule out the common dull ones. They are the cause nearly every time.
How common it is

Low back pain is among the most widespread health complaints in the world, and most adults experience it at some point. In the great majority of cases, no specific structural cause can be found, and doctors describe it as non-specific. That is reassuring. It means the pain usually does not signal serious damage. Most episodes improve substantially within a few weeks, whatever is done, though recurrences are common.
Keep moving

For decades, the standard advice for a sore back was bed rest. Research overturned it. Trials comparing rest with staying active found that people who continued with ordinary activity, within the limits of pain, recovered faster and had fewer long-term problems. Current guidelines in many countries recommend remaining active, returning to normal activities as soon as possible and using exercise as the main treatment. Hurting does not necessarily mean harming.
The myth of perfect posture

Many people believe that slouching damages the spine and that sitting bolt upright protects it. The evidence for this is weak. Studies have not found a consistent link between any particular sitting posture and back pain. The spine is a strong, adaptable structure built to bend. What seems to matter more is staying in any single position for a long time. Researchers and physiotherapists increasingly say that the best posture is the next one.
Break up sitting

The practical consequence is to change position often. Stand up at least every half hour, even for a minute. Walk to speak to a colleague. Take phone calls on your feet. Shift in your chair. A desk that adjusts between sitting and standing height helps mainly because it makes changing position easy, not because standing is better. Standing still all day brings problems of its own.
Setting up a desk

A comfortable arrangement reduces strain on the neck, shoulders and wrists. Place the top of the screen at about eye level and an arm's length away. Keep the keyboard and mouse close enough that your elbows stay near your sides, bent at roughly a right angle. Your feet should rest flat on the floor or on a support. A laptop used for hours needs a separate keyboard and a stand, since otherwise either the screen is too low or the keys are too high.
Lifting

For heavy objects, the familiar advice holds. Get close to the load, bend at the hips and knees, hold it near your body and avoid twisting while carrying. More important than technique is not lifting more than you are conditioned for. Backs become robust through gradual, regular loading, which is why strength training is protective. People who are generally strong and active are less likely to be troubled by back pain.
What helps

Exercise is the best-supported treatment for persistent back pain, and no one type has proved clearly superior. Walking, strengthening, stretching, yoga and swimming have all shown benefit. The best choice is whichever one you will keep doing. Heat can ease a sore back in the short term. Good sleep, lower stress and a healthy weight all help. Scans are seldom useful for ordinary back pain and often show harmless changes that cause needless worry.
When to seek help urgently

A few symptoms need prompt medical attention. Numbness around the groin or inner thighs, new difficulty passing urine or controlling the bowels, and weakness in the legs can indicate pressure on the nerves at the base of the spine and are an emergency. Pain after a serious fall or accident, pain with fever or unexplained weight loss, and severe pain that worsens at night should be assessed by a doctor.
Epictetus

Epictetus was born into slavery around the year 50 and later gained his freedom and taught philosophy in Rome and then in Greece. He wrote nothing himself. A student recorded his teaching, and a short handbook drawn from those notes opens with the idea for which he is best known. Some things are within our power, and some are not. Peace of mind, he taught, depends on keeping the two apart and concerning ourselves only with the first.
The two lists

What is within our power, according to the Stoics, is our own judgements, intentions, desires and actions: how we interpret events and what we choose to do. What is not is everything else. Our bodies, our possessions, our reputations, other people's behaviour, the weather, the past and the outcome of our efforts are all influenced by forces beyond us. We can affect some of these. We do not control them.
Where suffering comes from

The Stoic claim is that distress arises when we treat things on the second list as though they were on the first. We demand that other people approve of us, that a plan succeed, that we never fall ill. Since none of these can be guaranteed, the demand ensures frustration and anxiety. If instead we attach our sense of success to what we actually control, our own effort and conduct, we can be disappointed but not undone.
The archer

A favourite Stoic illustration is an archer. The archer can choose the bow, train diligently, aim carefully and release cleanly. Once the arrow has left the string, a gust of wind or a movement of the target may spoil the shot. A Stoic archer aims to shoot well, and regards hitting the target as preferred but not essential. The goal is redefined as doing one's own part excellently. The result is welcomed or accepted, whichever it turns out to be.
It is not passivity

This is sometimes misread as resignation. The Stoics were not quietists. Marcus Aurelius, who wrote the private notes known as the Meditations, governed the Roman Empire and commanded its armies. The teaching is to act as vigorously as you can on what you can influence while not staking your peace on the outcome. Nor does it mean suppressing feeling. It concerns the judgements that produce needless suffering, not ordinary grief or affection.
Events and opinions

A related teaching is that people are disturbed less by events than by their opinions about events. Two people stuck in the same delayed train have the same circumstances. One is furious and the other reads a book. The difference lies in what each tells themselves about the delay. The founders of modern cognitive therapy in the twentieth century acknowledged this idea as an ancestor of their approach, which treats distress by examining the thoughts behind it.
Rehearsing difficulty

The Stoics also recommended imagining setbacks in advance: the loss of a job, an illness, the failure of a venture. The purpose was not gloom. It was to reduce the shock when misfortune arrives, to appreciate what one has while one has it, and to notice that most feared outcomes could be endured. A few minutes spent calmly picturing how you would cope with a feared event often shrinks it to a manageable size.
Trying it

When something is troubling you, write it down and divide it. On one side, list the parts you control: what you will do, say and attend to. On the other, the parts you do not. Give your energy to the first list, and practise letting the second be what it is. The exercise takes a few minutes and clarifies more than hours of worry. It is very old advice, and it has lasted because it works for many people.
Where the profit comes from

Bluffs are memorable, but most of a winning player's income is value: betting the best hand and having a worse one call. At low and middle stakes, where opponents call too often, this is overwhelmingly true. A player who never bluffed but extracted full value from every strong hand would beat most casual games comfortably. A player who bluffs brilliantly but checks back winning hands on the river leaves money behind every session.
The test

A value bet is correct when, among the hands that will call you, more than half are worse than yours. The question to ask before betting is concrete: which worse hands call this bet? If you can name several likely holdings that are behind you and would pay, bet. If the only hands that call are ones that beat you, the bet achieves nothing. Worse hands fold, better hands call, and you lose the most when you lose.
Thin value

The skill that separates good players from average ones is betting hands that are only modestly strong. This is called thin value. Top pair with a middling kicker on the river, or second pair against an opponent who called twice with what looks like a draw that missed and a pair that did not. Average players check these hands, glad to reach showdown. Strong players bet a small amount and are called by weaker pairs often enough to profit.
Why players miss it

The barrier is fear. Betting a medium hand feels risky because sometimes you will be raised or shown a better hand, and those moments are vivid. The many times a worse hand quietly calls a small bet are less memorable. It helps to accept in advance that a correct thin value bet will run into a better hand a fair share of the time. If you are never called by better when you bet the river, you are not betting enough hands.
Size to the caller

The right amount is the largest your opponent's worse hands will pay. Against someone who hates folding any pair, bet big with strong hands, since the size barely affects whether they call. Against a cautious player, a smaller bet is called far more often and earns more on average. Think about what specific hands you are targeting. If you want a call from a weak top pair, do not bet an amount that only two pair would consider.
Do not slow play by default

Checking a strong hand to trap is tempting and usually costs money. It gives free cards to hands that could beat you, and it fails to build a pot. A big hand wants a big pot, and pots are built by betting on every street. Slow playing has a place on very dry boards against aggressive opponents who will bet if you check. Against passive players who call but rarely bet, checking a strong hand just means winning less.
The river check behind

The opposite error is betting a hand that cannot be called by worse. On the river with a medium-strength hand in position, such as a weak pair when the draws have missed, ask the test question honestly. If your opponent's worse hands are busted draws that will fold, and their better hands will call, then check and take the showdown. Betting there turns a hand with real value into a bluff that only gets called when it loses.
A session drill

For one session, at every river where you hold a made hand and it is your turn to bet, silently name three worse hands that would call. If you can, bet. If you cannot, check. Afterwards, note the hands where you checked and won against something that would have paid. Those are your missed bets. Most players find several a night, and adding them back is one of the quickest ways to raise a win rate.
Two curves

Demand describes how much of something buyers want at each price. As a rule, the lower the price, the more they want. Supply describes how much sellers are willing to offer at each price. As a rule, the higher the price, the more they offer. There is one price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. Markets tend toward that price, without anyone being in charge of finding it.
How the price is found

If the price is above that level, sellers offer more than buyers want. Unsold goods pile up, and sellers cut prices to move them. If the price is below it, buyers want more than is available. Shelves empty, queues form and sellers find they can charge more. The price settles where neither pressure remains. No one needs to know the whole picture. Each buyer and seller responds only to the price in front of them.
Shifts

Prices change when something moves one of the curves. A fashion for a product, rising incomes or a higher price for a substitute increases demand, and the price rises. A good harvest, a new production method or new competitors increase supply, and the price falls. A frost that destroys part of a coffee crop reduces supply and raises the price of coffee everywhere. Most business news about prices is a story about one of these shifts.
Elasticity

How strongly buyers react to a price change is called the price elasticity of demand. If a 10 percent rise in price causes people to buy 20 percent less, demand is elastic. If it causes them to buy only 2 percent less, demand is inelastic. The difference matters enormously to sellers. With elastic demand, raising the price reduces total revenue. With inelastic demand, raising the price increases it.
What makes demand inelastic

Three things make buyers insensitive to price. The good is a necessity. There are no close substitutes. And it takes a small share of the buyer's budget. Petrol in the short run fits the first two: people must still get to work, and the car they own runs on nothing else, so a large price rise cuts consumption only slightly. Salt fits all three. A particular brand of breakfast cereal fits none, since a dozen alternatives sit beside it.
Time changes everything

Demand becomes more elastic as time passes. When fuel prices rise, drivers can do little at first. Over several years they buy more efficient cars, move closer to work or change how they travel, and consumption falls much further. Supply behaves the same way. In the short run, a farmer cannot grow more wheat than was planted. Given a few seasons of high prices, more land is sown. This is why price spikes in commodities tend to be sharp and temporary.
Volatile markets

When both supply and demand are inelastic, small disturbances produce large price swings. If buyers must have the product and sellers cannot quickly produce more, a modest shortfall requires a big price rise to bring the two back into balance. Oil, electricity, some foods and housing in constrained cities behave this way. Markets where buyers can easily switch and sellers can easily expand, such as most manufactured goods, have far steadier prices.
What prices do

A price is a signal and an incentive at once. A rising price tells buyers to economize and tells producers to supply more, without either needing to know why the shortage arose. When prices are prevented from moving, the adjustment must happen in another way, usually through queues, shortages or surpluses. Whether to accept those effects in exchange for other goals, such as affordability or fairness, is a matter for politics. The mechanism itself is not seriously disputed.
The problem with tubes

Before the transistor, electronic equipment relied on vacuum tubes: glass bulbs in which a heated filament released electrons that a small voltage could control. Tubes could amplify signals and act as switches, which made radio, long-distance telephone calls and the first computers possible. They were also bulky, fragile, hot and hungry for power, and they burned out like light bulbs. An early American computer of 1945 used about 18,000 of them and consumed as much electricity as a small town.
Bell Labs

The telephone company's research arm, Bell Laboratories, wanted something better for its vast network of amplifiers and switches. After the Second World War it set up a group to study semiconductors, materials such as germanium and silicon that conduct electricity better than insulators and worse than metals. The group was led by William Shockley and included the theorist John Bardeen and the experimenter Walter Brattain.
December 1947

Bardeen and Brattain found that two closely spaced gold contacts pressed onto a piece of germanium could make a small current control a larger one. In December 1947 they demonstrated the device to their managers by amplifying a voice. It was named the transistor. Shockley, displeased at having been left out of the breakthrough, worked intensely over the following weeks and devised a more robust and practical design. The three shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956.
Out of the laboratory

The first widely sold product built on the new device was a pocket radio that went on sale in the United States in 1954. Japanese firms soon led the market, and the word transistor came to mean a small radio. Computers began to switch from tubes to transistors later in the decade. They became smaller, cooler and far more reliable. But every transistor still had to be made separately and wired to the others by hand.
The integrated circuit

The answer was to make many transistors and their connections together on one piece of semiconductor. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built the first working example in 1958. Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor independently devised a version using flat layers of silicon that proved far easier to manufacture. The integrated circuit, or chip, removed the hand wiring and opened the way to putting more and more transistors on each one.
Moore's observation

In 1965 Gordon Moore, a colleague of Noyce, noted that the number of components on a chip had been doubling every year and predicted the trend would continue. He later adjusted the pace to every two years. For more than half a century the industry kept roughly to that curve. A chip of the early 1970s held a few thousand transistors. A processor in a current phone holds well over ten billion.
The type that won

Nearly all of those are a kind called the MOSFET, first built at Bell Labs in 1959. It is controlled by voltage, uses very little power and can be made extremely small. The dimensions of the smallest features on today's chips are measured in billionths of a metre. By some estimates, more MOSFETs have been manufactured than any other object, a number written with more than twenty digits.
What it made possible

Each time transistors shrank, they became cheaper, faster and less power-hungry, and something new became practical: the pocket calculator, the personal computer, the mobile phone, the internet and the present generation of artificial intelligence. Few inventions have reshaped so much in so short a time. The same tiny switch, endlessly multiplied, is the basis of almost every electronic device. It began as a patch of germanium, a scrap of gold foil and a plastic wedge.
Voltage comes from chemistry

A battery cell produces a voltage set by the materials inside it, not by its size. An alkaline cell gives about 1.5 volts whether it is a small AAA or a large D. A nickel metal hydride rechargeable gives about 1.2. A lithium-ion cell gives a nominal 3.6 or 3.7. A lead-acid cell gives about 2.1, and six in series make the familiar 12 volt car battery. To get more voltage, cells are stacked in series. Size affects only how long the cell lasts.
Capacity

Capacity is measured in amp hours or milliamp hours: current multiplied by time. A good AA alkaline holds roughly 2,000 to 3,000 milliamp hours at low drain. A common cylindrical lithium-ion cell holds 2,500 to 3,500. A coin cell of the CR2032 type holds only about 220. To compare batteries of different voltages fairly, multiply capacity by voltage to get watt hours, which is the stored energy.
Voltage sags as you use it

A battery's voltage is not constant. An alkaline cell starts above 1.5 volts and declines steadily toward 1.0 as it empties, so devices that need a firm 1.5 volts quit while much of the energy remains. Lithium-ion holds a flatter voltage through most of its discharge, from 4.2 volts when full to about 3.0 when empty. This is why a fuel gauge based on voltage alone works tolerably for alkaline cells and poorly for lithium ones.
Internal resistance

Every battery behaves as if it had a small resistor in series with it. When you draw current, some voltage is lost across that internal resistance, and the battery warms. Alkaline cells have fairly high internal resistance, so they perform poorly in high-drain devices such as camera flashes, delivering a fraction of their rated capacity. Rechargeable cells have much lower internal resistance and handle heavy loads far better, despite their lower nominal voltage.
The C rate

Charge and discharge currents are often quoted relative to capacity. A rate of 1C means a current that would empty the battery in one hour. For a 2,000 milliamp hour cell, 1C is 2 amps, and half that rate is 1 amp. Each cell type has limits. Ordinary lithium-ion cells are typically charged at half C to 1C. Cells built for power tools and drones can discharge at 10C or more. Exceeding the rating overheats the cell.
Lithium needs respect

Lithium-ion cells store a great deal of energy in a small space, several times more per kilogram than lead-acid. They must be kept within strict limits. Charged above about 4.2 volts, discharged below about 2.5 to 3, short-circuited or punctured, they can overheat and catch fire. Nearly every pack includes a protection circuit, and they need a charger designed for the chemistry. Do not charge them when they are below freezing. A swollen cell should be retired at once.
Making them last

Rechargeable batteries wear out with use and with time. For lithium-ion, heat is the main enemy, followed by being held at full charge. A laptop kept plugged in at 100 percent in a warm room ages faster than one cycled between 30 and 80 percent. For long storage, leave lithium cells at around half charge in a cool place. Nickel metal hydride cells of the low self-discharge type hold most of their charge for a year on the shelf.
Choosing for a project

For a device that sips power for months, such as a remote control or a clock, alkaline cells are cheap and simple. For anything used daily with moderate drain, low self-discharge nickel metal hydride cells pay for themselves quickly. For compact, high-energy designs, lithium-ion or lithium polymer with a proper charging and protection module is standard. For large amounts of energy where weight does not matter, lead-acid remains cheap and forgiving.
What detergent does

Laundry detergent has several working ingredients. Surfactants loosen oily dirt and hold it in the water so that it rinses away. Builders soften the water, which lets the surfactants work properly. Many detergents contain enzymes, biological catalysts that break down particular kinds of stain: one kind for proteins such as blood and egg, another for starches, another for fats. Optical brighteners are added to make whites appear brighter under daylight.
Cold water works

Heating water accounts for most of the energy a washing machine uses, about nine tenths by the estimate of the American energy efficiency programme. Modern detergents and their enzymes are formulated to work in cool water, and most everyday loads come out just as clean. Cold washing is also gentler, with less fading and shrinking. Hot water is still worth using for towels, bedding and heavily soiled items, and for anything used by someone who has been ill.
Less detergent than you think

Using more detergent does not produce cleaner clothes. Excess is not fully rinsed out. It leaves a residue that stiffens fabric, traps dirt and odours and builds up inside the machine. Modern machines use little water, and concentrated detergents need only a small measure. Follow the dosing lines on the cap, adjusted for load size, soil and water hardness. If towels feel stiff or the machine smells musty, too much detergent is a likely cause.
Sorting

Sort by colour and by fabric. New dark and brightly dyed items release dye for their first several washes and will tint anything pale. Wash whites, lights and darks separately. Heavy items such as jeans and towels abrade delicate fabrics and should not share a load with them. Close zips so they do not snag other garments, and turn printed shirts and dark jeans inside out to reduce fading.
Stains

Treat a stain as soon as you can, before it dries. Blot, do not rub. Rinse from the back of the fabric with cold water to push the stain out the way it came in. Protein stains such as blood, egg and milk must be treated cold, since hot water sets them permanently. Oily stains respond to a drop of washing-up liquid worked in before washing. Check that the stain has gone before using a dryer, because heat fixes whatever remains.
The care label

The symbols on a garment's label form a small language. A tub shape gives the washing instructions, with a number for the maximum temperature in Celsius or dots for heat level, and a hand in the tub meaning hand wash. A triangle concerns bleach. A square concerns drying, with a circle inside it for tumble drying. An iron shape gives ironing heat by its dots. A plain circle means professional cleaning. A cross through any symbol means do not.
Drying

Tumble drying is hard on clothes. The lint in the filter is fibre that has been worn off the fabric. High heat shrinks cotton and damages the elastic in underwear and sportswear. Use the lowest heat that does the job and take clothes out while slightly damp. Line or rack drying costs nothing and extends the life of garments. Wool shrinks through a combination of heat, moisture and agitation, which is why it is washed cool and laid flat.
Looking after the machine

A washing machine needs occasional attention. Leave the door and detergent drawer open between washes so that the interior can dry, which discourages mould on the door seal. Run an empty hot cycle every month or so to clear residue. Clean the drain filter a few times a year. Empty the dryer's lint filter after every load, both for efficiency and because accumulated lint is a recognized cause of house fires.
Why it usually fails

Telling someone their presentation was weak, or that they need to be more professional, gives them nothing to work with. They know you are displeased. They do not know what to change. Because the remark is about them and not about anything in particular, it feels like a judgement of character, and people defend their character. The usual result is resentment and no improvement. Vague praise fails in a similar way: pleasant and uninformative.
Describe the behaviour

Useful feedback names something the person did that an observer could have seen or heard. Not you were disorganized, which is a conclusion, but the report arrived two days after the date we agreed. Not you are careless, but there were four arithmetic errors in the summary table. A description of behaviour can be discussed and corrected. A label can only be accepted or rejected, and it will nearly always be rejected.
Situation, behaviour, impact

One widely taught structure has three parts. First state the situation: when and where. Then the behaviour: what the person did. Then the impact: the effect it had on you, the team or the work. In Tuesday's client meeting, you interrupted the client twice while she was describing the problem, and she stopped offering details. Each part is a fact or a first-hand observation. The listener may not like it, and they cannot easily dispute it.
Say it soon

Feedback loses value with every day that passes. The details fade for both of you, and the person may repeat the behaviour in the meantime. Saving up criticism for an annual review is nearly useless, and it arrives as an ambush. The best moment is as soon as you can speak privately and calmly. If you are angry, wait until you are not, since anger turns a description into an accusation, but do not wait a month.
In private, and ask first

Criticism delivered in front of others adds humiliation, and the person will remember that and nothing else. Praise can be public. Correction should not be. It also helps to ask before beginning: may I give you some thoughts on the meeting? The question takes two seconds, gives the other person a moment to prepare and some sense of control, and makes it far more likely that they will listen instead of bracing for a blow.
Look forward

Having described what happened, turn to what should happen next. What would you like them to do differently? Better still, ask what they think. People are more committed to solutions they have proposed themselves. A conversation that ends with a specific change agreed on both sides has succeeded. One that ends with the person merely feeling bad has achieved nothing, however accurate the criticism was.
Praise needs the same precision

Specific positive feedback is as valuable as specific criticism and far rarer. Good job tells someone only that you are pleased. Saying that the way they summarized the three options on one page let the committee decide in ten minutes tells them exactly what to do again. People repeat what they understand to have worked. If you want more of a behaviour, describe it as carefully as you would describe a fault.
Receiving it

The other half of the skill is taking feedback well. When someone criticizes your work, the instinct is to explain or defend. Resist it. Listen to the end. Ask a question to make sure you understand, and ask for an example if none was given. Thank them, since it took some effort to say. You can decide afterwards how much of it you agree with. People who react defensively soon stop being told anything.
What it is

A check-raise is exactly what the name says. You check, your opponent bets, and you raise. It was once considered so underhanded that some card rooms banned it. Today it is standard and essential. The player who acts first is at a disadvantage on every street. The check-raise is the tool that offsets it, because it allows the first player to trap bets that the second player makes simply because they were checked to.
Why not just bet

When you are out of position against the player who raised before the flop, that player will bet a large share of flops whatever they hold. If you bet first with a strong hand, they fold their misses and you win a small pot. If you check, they bet their misses, and now your raise captures that extra money. Checking lets them put chips in with hands that would never have called a bet. The check-raise wins bigger pots with the same cards.
For value

The foundation is strong hands: two pair, sets, and top pair with a good kicker on boards where opponents will continue with worse. On wet boards, raising also charges the many draws that would otherwise see the next card cheaply. Size the raise to about three times your opponent's bet, somewhat more if you will be out of position for the rest of the hand and the board is full of draws. A tiny raise gives every draw the right price.
As a semi-bluff

If you only check-raise strong hands, attentive opponents will fold whenever you do it. So add draws. A flush draw, an open-ended straight draw, or a gutshot with two overcards all make good candidates. These hands can win immediately when the opponent folds, and they can still win by improving when called. A draw played this way earns far more than a draw played by calling and hoping, because it has two ways to succeed.
Choosing the board

The play works best on flops that favour the caller's range: low and middling connected boards such as seven, six, four or eight, five, three. The preflop raiser's big cards have mostly missed, and you can credibly hold two pair, sets and straights. On boards with an ace or king, the raiser's range is strong and yours is not, so check-raising as a bluff there is expensive. Match the play to boards where the strong hands are plausibly yours.
Against the right player

Check-raising needs an opponent who bets when checked to. Against someone who makes a continuation bet on nearly every flop, it is very profitable, as their betting range is full of air. Against a passive player who only bets strong hands, checking a big hand risks giving a free card, so simply bet. And if a tight, passive player check-raises you, believe them. At low stakes, that line is a strong hand far more often than not.
After you raise

Have a plan for the turn. If called, your opponent usually has a pair or a draw. With a strong made hand, keep betting, sized to the wetness of the board. With a semi-bluff, continue on cards that improve your hand or that are bad for your opponent's likely holdings, and be willing to give up on blanks. The mistake to avoid is automatic follow-through. A second and third bet with nothing must have a reason behind it.
Defending against it

When you are the one check-raised, the answer depends on who did it and on what board. Against aggressive players on draw-heavy boards, continue with your good pairs and your own draws, since they are bluffing some of the time. Against passive players, fold all but your strongest hands. You can also reduce your exposure in advance by checking back some flops, which removes the weak bets that a check-raise feeds on.
Pooling risk

Insurance works by pooling. A thousand households each face a small chance of a house fire in a given year. For any one of them, the loss would be ruinous. For the group, the number of fires is fairly predictable. Each household pays a modest premium, and the pooled money rebuilds the few houses that burn. An unpredictable catastrophe for the individual is turned into a small, certain cost shared by all.
You should expect to lose

Premiums must cover the claims paid out plus the insurer's staff, offices, advertising and profit. So customers as a group pay in more than they get back. Measured purely by expected value, buying insurance is a losing bet. That is not a criticism. You are paying a fee to be rid of a risk you could not bear. The purchase makes sense when the possible loss would wreck your finances and little sense when it would not.
Insure against ruin

The principle that follows is to insure against losses you could not absorb and to carry the rest yourself. A house burning down, a serious illness or injury, being held liable for harming someone else, or the death or disability of a family's earner are all capable of destroying a household's finances. These are worth insuring fully. A cracked phone screen or a failed toaster is an annoyance that savings can cover.
Small policies are poor value

Extended warranties on appliances and electronics, insurance on individual gadgets and similar small policies are generally expensive relative to the risk they cover, since sales commissions and administration absorb much of the premium. Consumer organizations have long advised against most of them. If you decline all such offers and put the money aside, you will almost certainly come out ahead over the years, and you will have the cash for the occasional repair.
Deductibles

The deductible, or excess, is the part of any claim you pay yourself. A higher one lowers the premium, often considerably, because it removes the small claims that are costly for an insurer to process. This is the same principle again. Choose the highest deductible you could comfortably pay from savings, and let the policy protect you against the large losses. An emergency fund and a high deductible work well together.
Problems insurers face

Two difficulties shape every policy. People who know they are at higher risk are keener to buy cover, which pushes up the average cost. Insurers respond with questionnaires, medical checks and exclusions. And people who are insured may take less care, since someone else will pay. Insurers respond with deductibles and conditions. Much of the fine print that irritates customers exists to manage these two problems.
Reading a policy

Three items deserve attention before you buy. The limit is the most the insurer will pay, and it should match the loss you actually face. The exclusions list what is not covered, and floods, earthquakes and wear are commonly left out of standard home policies. The basis of payment says whether you receive what an item would cost to replace or only its depreciated value. Comparing quotes on price alone, without these, compares different products.
A sensible approach

List the events that could seriously damage your finances and check that each is covered up to a realistic amount. For most households, that means health, home or contents, motor liability, and life and disability cover if others depend on your income. Raise deductibles to what you can afford. Decline cover for small things. Review the whole arrangement every couple of years or after any major change in your life, and seek qualified advice when the amounts are large.
Circuits and packets

The old telephone network connected two callers by reserving a continuous path between them for the whole call. That is wasteful for computers, which send data in short bursts. In the 1960s, researchers in the United States and Britain independently proposed another approach. Break each message into small blocks, label each with its destination and let them find their own way across a shared network. The British researcher Donald Davies called the blocks packets.
The first network

The idea was first tried on a large scale in a network funded by the American defence research agency and called ARPANET. On October 29, 1969, a computer at the University of California in Los Angeles sent the first message to another at a research institute several hundred kilometres north. The operator was typing the word login. The system crashed after two letters. Within a few years, the network linked dozens of universities and laboratories.
A common language

Other networks appeared, each with its own rules, and they could not talk to one another. In the 1970s, Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn designed a set of rules, or protocols, that allowed separate networks to be joined into one. ARPANET adopted them on January 1, 1983, a date often given as the birth of the internet. The name itself comes from the idea of a network of networks.
Addresses and routers

Every device connected to the internet has a numerical address. Every packet carries the address it came from and the address it is going to. Between networks sit specialized computers called routers. A router reads the destination on each arriving packet and forwards it one step closer, using a table of routes it keeps updated by exchanging information with its neighbours. No router knows the whole path. Each knows only the next hop.
Different routes, one message

Packets belonging to the same message may take different paths and arrive out of order, and some may be lost. A second layer of rules deals with that. The receiving computer checks the packets, puts them back in sequence and asks for any that are missing to be sent again. The sender also slows down when the network is congested. A photograph or a web page is thus rebuilt exactly from fragments that crossed the world separately.
Names

People prefer names to numbers. A worldwide directory called the domain name system translates a name typed into a browser into the numerical address of the computer that holds the site. Your device asks a nearby directory server, which asks others if it does not know, and the answer comes back in a fraction of a second. The system was introduced in the 1980s and is consulted billions of times a day.
The physical network

For all the talk of clouds, the internet is a physical thing. Nearly all traffic between continents travels as pulses of light through fibre-optic cables laid on the sea bed, each about as thick as a garden hose. Satellites carry a small share. On land, the fibres run alongside railways, roads and pipelines to buildings where networks interconnect. A ship's anchor dragging across a cable can slow the connections of an entire country.
Nobody is in charge

There is no central control room. The internet is tens of thousands of independently owned networks that have agreed to use the same protocols and to carry one another's traffic. Technical standards are set by open bodies of engineers. The World Wide Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee around 1990, is one application that runs on top of this foundation, as are email and video calls. The design's lack of a centre is the source of both its resilience and its disorder.
Voltages as bits

A digital signal carries information as one of two states, high or low, usually written 1 and 0. Physically, these are voltage ranges. In a 5 volt system, a voltage near 5 is high and near zero is low. In a 3.3 volt system, high is near 3.3. Most modern microcontrollers and sensors use 3.3 volts or lower, because lower voltages save power and suit smaller transistors. Older designs and many hobby boards still use 5.
The thresholds

A chip does not require exactly 5 volts or exactly zero. It has thresholds. For a typical 3.3 volt part, anything above about 2 volts is guaranteed to be read as high and anything below about 0.8 volts as low. Between them lies an undefined band where the result is not promised. The gap between what an output delivers and what an input requires is the noise margin, and it is what makes digital circuits tolerant of interference.
Floating inputs

An input pin connected to nothing is not at zero. It is floating. Modern inputs draw almost no current, so the pin's voltage is set by stray electric fields from nearby wires, the mains and even your hand moving past. It drifts unpredictably between high and low. A circuit with a floating input may work on the bench and fail when you lean over it. Every input must be driven to a defined level at all times.
Pull-up and pull-down resistors

The standard cure is a resistor that gently holds the pin at a known level when nothing else is driving it. A pull-up connects the pin to the supply. A pull-down connects it to ground. A push button then needs only to connect the pin to the opposite level when pressed. The usual value is around 10 kilohms: low enough to hold the pin firmly, high enough that little current is wasted while the button is held.
Built-in pull-ups

Most microcontrollers contain optional pull-up resistors on their input pins, switched on in software. They are typically in the range of 20 to 50 kilohms. Enabling one saves an external part. The consequence is that the logic reads backwards from what beginners expect. With a pull-up, the pin reads high when the button is not pressed and low when it is. This arrangement is called active low and is extremely common.
Mixing 5 and 3.3 volts

Connecting parts that run at different voltages needs care in one direction. A 3.3 volt output driving a 5 volt input often works, since 3.3 volts is above the high threshold of many 5 volt inputs, though not all. A 5 volt output driving a 3.3 volt input can damage it, unless the datasheet states that the pin tolerates 5 volts. In that direction, use a voltage divider for slow signals or a level shifter chip for fast or two-way ones.
Outputs that only pull down

Some outputs are open drain, meaning they can connect the line to ground but cannot drive it high. They rely on a pull-up resistor to bring the line up when released. This allows several devices to share one wire safely, since none can fight another by driving high while it drives low. The I2C bus works this way. If a line of this kind is stuck low or never goes high, a missing pull-up is the first thing to check.
How much a pin can drive

A logic output is a signal source, not a power supply. A typical microcontroller pin can safely source or sink something on the order of 10 to 20 milliamps, with a lower limit on the total across all pins. That is enough for an LED with its resistor and not enough for a motor, a relay coil or a strip of lights. Anything heavier needs a transistor or driver chip between the pin and the load.
What a wall is made of

Most modern interior walls are sheets of plasterboard, also called drywall, fixed to a frame of vertical timbers called studs. The board itself is a soft, chalky material faced with paper. It will hold a nail well enough for a small picture and almost nothing heavier. Anything with real weight has to be fixed either into a stud or with a fixing designed to spread the load across the back of the board.
Finding the studs

In North American houses, studs are usually spaced 16 inches apart, measured centre to centre, and each is about an inch and a half wide. Electrical boxes for sockets and switches are normally fixed to the side of a stud, which gives you a starting point to measure from. Knocking on the wall produces a hollow sound between studs and a duller one over them. An electronic stud finder, or a small strong magnet that locates the screws holding the board, is more reliable.
Light loads

For a framed picture of a few kilograms, a picture hook with a nail driven in at a downward angle is enough, even into plasterboard alone. Galleries commonly hang work so that its centre is about 145 centimetres, or 57 inches, from the floor, roughly eye level for an average adult. Measure, mark lightly in pencil and use a spirit level for anything wide. Two hooks set apart keep a frame from tilting.
Medium loads

For mirrors, small shelves and curtain rails, where no stud is conveniently placed, use a wall anchor. Simple plastic plugs that expand as a screw is driven in are suitable only for light items. Self-drilling anchors with coarse threads hold more. Toggle bolts, which pass through a hole and open out behind the board like wings, spread the load widely and hold considerably more. The packaging states a rated load, which should comfortably exceed the weight to be hung.
Heavy loads

Televisions, large shelves loaded with books, wall cabinets and anything a person might pull on should be screwed into studs with long, substantial screws that pass through the board and well into the timber. A wall bracket for a television is designed to span two studs. If the studs are not where you need them, fix a horizontal timber or metal rail across two studs first and mount to that.
Masonry is different

Solid walls of brick, block or concrete require a different approach. A hammer drill with a masonry bit makes the hole. A plastic or nylon plug of the correct size is tapped in, and the screw expands it against the sides of the hole. Drill into the brick or block itself, not into the softer mortar between. The plug, the drill bit and the screw must match, and the sizes are printed on the packet.
What not to drill into

Cables and pipes run inside walls. Electrical cables generally travel vertically above and below sockets and switches, and horizontally at the level of sockets, so avoid drilling directly in line with them. Pipes are likely near sinks, baths and radiators. Many stud finders include a setting that detects live cables and metal. Drill only as deep as you need. A piece of tape wrapped around the bit makes a simple depth marker.
A few good habits

Hold an envelope or a folded sticky note beneath the drill to catch the dust. Drill a narrow pilot hole before driving a large screw into timber, to prevent splitting. Fit the screws loosely, check with the level, then tighten. Test the fixing by pulling down on it firmly before trusting it with something that matters. If you rent your home, check what your agreement says about making holes before you begin.
Hearing is not listening

In an ordinary conversation, a great deal of attention goes to things other than the speaker. You are planning your reply, judging what was said, recalling a similar story of your own or waiting for a gap. People speak at perhaps 150 words a minute, and the mind works much faster, so there is spare capacity that readily wanders. The speaker usually senses it. Being half heard is among the commonest complaints in marriages and workplaces.
Listening to understand

The psychologist Carl Rogers, working in the 1940s and 50s, argued that the most helpful thing one person can do for another in conversation is to try to grasp the other's meaning from their point of view, without judging it. He and a colleague called this active listening. The listener's task is not to fix, advise or evaluate. It is to understand accurately and to show that they have. Simple as that sounds, few people do it.
Reflecting back

The central technique is to restate what you heard in your own words and check it. So the deadline itself is not the problem, it is that nobody told you it had moved. If you are right, the speaker feels understood and goes further. If you are wrong, they correct you, and you have avoided a misunderstanding. It can feel artificial at first. Done sincerely and not mechanically, it is rarely noticed as a technique at all.
Ask open questions

Questions that can be answered with yes or no shut a conversation down. Questions beginning with what or how open it up. What happened next? How did that affect you? What do you make of it? Be careful with why, which can sound like a demand for justification. A good question follows from what the person has just said, which also proves that you were paying attention. Questions that steer toward your own view are advice in disguise.
Leave silence alone

Most people find a pause of three or four seconds uncomfortable and rush to fill it. Experienced interviewers, counsellors and negotiators do the opposite. When the speaker stops, they wait. Very often the speaker continues, and what comes after the pause is more candid than what came before. Silence signals that you are not in a hurry and that there is room for more. Learning to tolerate it is one of the simplest improvements a listener can make.
Hold the advice

When someone describes a problem, the urge to offer a solution is strong. Frequently they have not asked for one. They may have thought of your suggestion already. They may want to think aloud, or simply to be heard. Jumping to advice can imply that the problem is easy and they should have solved it. If you are unsure what is wanted, ask: would it help to talk through options, or do you mainly want me to listen?
Remove the distractions

Attention is visible. Turning to face someone, looking at them and putting away the phone all communicate that they matter. A phone lying on the table between two people, even untouched, is a reminder that the conversation can be interrupted at any moment. If you truly cannot give someone your attention now, it is better to say so and name a time when you can than to offer a distracted half of it.
What it gets you

People tell good listeners more. They bring bad news earlier, admit mistakes sooner and explain what they actually want. In disputes, being accurately heard often lowers the temperature more than any concession does, since much anger is the frustration of not being understood. Try it once this week. In one conversation, do nothing but ask, reflect and wait. Notice how much longer the other person talks and how much you learn.
Why bluff at all

If you only bet with strong hands, observant opponents stop paying you. They fold when you bet and take the pot when you check. Bluffing is what forces them to call your value bets. In theory, the right mix of bluffs and value hands leaves your opponent with no profitable response. In practice, at most tables, bluffing is a tool to use selectively against players who fold too much and to put away against players who do not.
The ratio on the river

On the last street there is a clean relationship between bet size and how many bluffs you can include. When you bet the size of the pot, your opponent is getting 2 to 1 and needs to win a third of the time. So a balanced betting range has one bluff for every two value hands. With a bet of half the pot, the opponent gets 3 to 1, and the mix is one bluff for every three value hands. Bigger bets permit more bluffs.
Pick hands that cannot win otherwise

The best hands to bluff with are those with no chance at showdown. A missed draw that has become nine high cannot win by checking, so it loses nothing by bluffing. A hand such as third pair might win if checked, so turning it into a bluff wastes that value. This is the first filter. When choosing which of your weak hands to bet, start with the ones that are worthless if you check.
Blockers

The second filter is which cards you hold. If the board shows three spades and you hold the ace of spades with no flush, your opponent cannot have the best possible flush. That makes strong hands less likely in their range and folds more likely. A card that removes combinations of the hands you fear is a blocker. Good river bluffs block the hands that would call. Equally, avoid holding cards that block the missed draws your opponent would fold.
Tell a consistent story

A bluff must represent a specific strong hand, and your actions on earlier streets must fit it. If you called the flop and turn on a board with a flush draw and then bet big when the third suited card arrives, the story makes sense. If you checked twice and then bet big on a harmless river card, it does not. Before bluffing, ask what hand you are claiming to hold and whether you would have played that hand this way.
Bluff on early streets with equity

On the flop and turn, the best bluffs are semi-bluffs: draws and hands with overcards that can improve. They win when the opponent folds and still have a chance when called. Pure bluffs with no possibility of improving are better saved for the river, when all the cards are out. A sensible pattern is to bet many draws on the flop, continue with the better ones on the turn, and on the river bluff with those that missed.
Count the opponents

Each additional player in the pot makes a bluff less likely to work, since every one of them has to fold. A bluff that succeeds 50 percent of the time against one opponent might succeed 25 percent of the time against two with similar tendencies. Bluff mainly in pots with a single opponent. Against several, bet your real hands and your strong draws and let the rest go.
Most games are under-bluffed

All of this theory assumes an opponent who can fold. Many recreational players call far too often, driven by curiosity and by the fear of being bluffed. Against them, the right number of bluffs is close to zero, and the right response is to bet your good hands larger. The reverse also holds. At lower stakes, big bets and raises on the river are strong hands far more often than theory would predict. When a quiet player suddenly bets big, folding is usually right.
The method

Dollar-cost averaging means investing the same sum of money at fixed intervals, whatever the price happens to be. Three hundred dollars on the first of each month into the same fund, for example. You make no attempt to judge whether the market is high or low. The decision is made once and then carried out automatically. Anyone who contributes to a retirement plan from each pay cheque is already doing it.
A built-in advantage

Because the amount is fixed, it buys more units when the price is low and fewer when it is high. Suppose you invest 100 dollars in each of three months at prices of 10, 5 and 10 dollars. You buy 10 units, then 20, then 10. You hold 40 units for 300 dollars, an average cost of 7.50 each. The average price over the period was 8.33. Your cost is lower because your money automatically bought the most when the price was lowest.
The behavioural benefit

The larger advantage is psychological. Investors are tempted to wait for a better moment, to buy after prices have risen and to sell in a panic after they have fallen. An automatic schedule takes those decisions away. A falling market becomes a chance to buy more units for the same money. People who invest by standing order tend to keep going through downturns that drive others out of the market at the worst time.
With a lump sum

A different question arises when you already have a large sum, such as an inheritance. Should you invest it all now or feed it in over a year? A much-cited study by the fund company Vanguard, covering several decades of market history in three countries, found that investing at once did better about two thirds of the time. The reason is simple. Markets rise more often than they fall, so money waiting on the sidelines usually misses some growth.
Why people still phase it in

The remaining third of the time, investing all at once is followed by a fall, and the experience is painful. Spreading a lump sum over several months reduces the chance of that outcome and the regret that comes with it. It costs a little expected return in exchange for a calmer mind. If the alternative to phasing is being too anxious to invest at all, phasing is clearly the better course. Choose a schedule in advance and keep to it.
What it does not do

Dollar-cost averaging does not protect against loss. If the investment falls and stays down, you lose money, having bought all the way down. It does not improve a poor investment. And it works only if you continue during declines, which is when it feels worst and achieves most. Stopping contributions when prices fall throws away the whole advantage of the method.
Making it automatic

The practical value lies in removing yourself from the process. Arrange for the transfer to happen on the day you are paid, before the money can be spent elsewhere. Choose a low-cost, broadly diversified fund. Increase the amount when your income rises. Then look at the account rarely. The fewer decisions you have to take, the fewer opportunities there are to take a bad one.
The bigger picture

Arguments about the best timing involve small differences. How much you save, how long you remain invested and how little you pay in costs matter far more. A person who invests a modest amount every month for thirty years, in good markets and bad, will almost certainly do better than one who spends those years waiting for the ideal moment. A regular habit is unexciting, and that is its strength.
Half a position

A ship's latitude, its distance north or south of the equator, can be found by measuring the height of the Sun at noon or of certain stars at night. Sailors had done this for centuries. Longitude, the position east or west, was a different matter. With no way to measure it, navigators estimated it from speed, heading and time elapsed, a method called dead reckoning. Over weeks at sea, the errors grew to hundreds of kilometres.
The cost

The consequences were lethal. Ships missed islands where they needed to take on water, and crews died of scurvy on voyages that ran long. Ships struck coasts their captains believed were far away. In 1707 a British naval squadron returning from the Mediterranean ran onto rocks off the Scilly Isles in fog, having misjudged its position. Four ships sank, and well over a thousand men drowned. It was one of the worst disasters in British naval history.
The prize

In 1714 the British Parliament offered a reward of up to 20,000 pounds, a fortune at the time, for a practical method of finding longitude at sea to within half a degree. A board of scientists and naval officers was set up to judge proposals. Most learned opinion expected the answer to come from astronomy, by using the Moon's motion against the stars as a kind of celestial clock.
Why time is the answer

The Earth turns through 15 degrees of longitude every hour. So longitude is really a difference in time. If you know that it is noon where you are, by the Sun, and you know that at the same moment it is 2 in the afternoon at your home port, you are 30 degrees west of home. The entire difficulty was in knowing the time at home. That required a clock that would keep accurate time for months on a pitching, damp ship.
Harrison

No such clock existed. Pendulum clocks were useless at sea, and changes in temperature made springs run fast or slow. John Harrison, a carpenter and self-taught clockmaker from the north of England, devoted most of his life to the problem. Between the 1730s and 1750s he built three large and ingenious sea clocks. Then he changed course entirely and produced a fourth timekeeper that looked like an oversized pocket watch, about 13 centimetres across.
The trial

In 1761 Harrison's son carried the watch on a voyage from England to Jamaica. After 81 days at sea, it was found to be only about five seconds slow, a small fraction of the allowed error. The board was unconvinced and suspected luck. Its leading astronomers favoured the rival lunar method and demanded more trials and full disclosure of the mechanism. Harrison received his money in instalments over many years.
Vindication

Harrison was by then an old man. He appealed to King George III, who tested one of the watches himself and took up the case. In 1773 Parliament awarded Harrison most of the remaining sum. He died three years later. Meanwhile, Captain James Cook had taken a copy of the watch on his second voyage around the world and praised it as a trusty guide. Within a few decades, marine chronometers were standard equipment.
What remains

The lunar method was also made to work and was used alongside chronometers for a century, as it needed no costly instrument. In 1884 an international conference chose the line through the observatory at Greenwich, near London, as the world's zero of longitude. Satellite navigation has since replaced both methods. The principle is unchanged. A satellite receiver, like Harrison's watch, finds position by measuring time with great precision.
A computer in one package

A microcontroller combines a processor, memory for the program, working memory and a set of input and output circuits on a single chip. It is designed to be embedded in a product and do one job indefinitely: run a washing machine, read a thermostat, blink a bike light. A microprocessor, by contrast, is only the processor and needs separate memory and support chips. A modern car contains dozens of microcontrollers, and a typical home holds hundreds.
The processor core

The core fetches instructions from memory and executes them one after another. Small microcontrollers use simple cores, 8 bits or 32 bits wide, running at a few million to a few hundred million instructions per second. That is slow next to a laptop and more than enough to read a sensor and decide what to do thousands of times a second. The core in the chip at the heart of the classic Arduino Uno is an 8-bit design clocked at 16 megahertz.
Three kinds of memory

Flash memory holds the program and keeps it when power is removed. RAM holds variables while the program runs and is wiped at power-off. Many chips add a small amount of EEPROM for settings that must survive. The quantities are tiny by computer standards. The Arduino Uno's chip has 32 kilobytes of flash and just 2 kilobytes of RAM. Writing software for such a device means being careful with every byte.
Pins that do many jobs

General purpose input and output pins are the chip's contact with the world. Each can be set by software as an input, to read a switch or sensor, or as an output, to drive a signal high or low. Most pins have alternative functions as well, selected in software: a serial port, an analog input, a timer output. This is why the same chip can serve in thousands of different products with only the program changed.
Timers and counters

Hardware timers count clock ticks independently of the main program. They measure intervals, generate precisely timed pulses, produce the pulse-width signals that dim LEDs and steer servo motors, and wake the chip at set times. Because they run in hardware, their timing stays exact even while the processor is busy. A good deal of embedded programming consists of configuring timers correctly, and they are the first peripheral worth learning in depth.
Talking to analog and digital parts

An analog to digital converter turns a voltage on a pin into a number, which is how a microcontroller reads a temperature sensor or a battery level. Serial interfaces let it exchange data with other chips over two to four wires, using standards called UART, SPI and I2C. With those two capabilities, one small chip can read nearly any sensor and control displays, radios, memory cards and motor drivers.
Interrupts and sleep

An interrupt lets an event, such as a pin changing or a timer expiring, pause the main program and run a short routine immediately. This lets the chip respond in microseconds without constantly checking. Combined with sleep modes, in which most of the chip is switched off, it is the key to long battery life. A well-designed sensor node may sleep at a few millionths of an amp and wake for a few thousandths of a second each minute.
Choosing one

For learning, pick a board with good documentation and a large community before worrying about specifications. Classic 8-bit Arduino boards are simple and forgiving. Boards based on 32-bit chips offer far more speed and memory for similar money. Some, such as the ESP32 family, include Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios on the chip. The skills transfer between all of them. Pins, timers, converters and serial ports work on the same principles everywhere.
Why own tools

A great many household tasks are simple: tightening a loose hinge, assembling furniture, hanging a shelf, replacing a tap washer, bleeding a radiator. They become difficult only without the right tool. A basic kit turns these from problems into ten-minute jobs. It does not need to be large or expensive. A dozen well-chosen tools kept together in one box will handle the great majority of what an ordinary home requires.
Screwdrivers

Start with screwdrivers, since screws hold most things together. You need at least two cross-head drivers and two flat ones in different sizes, or one handle with interchangeable bits. The driver must fit the screw snugly. One that is too small will slip and chew up the head, after which the screw is very hard to remove. Press firmly as you turn. Clockwise tightens and anticlockwise loosens, with rare exceptions.
Hammer and pliers

A claw hammer of medium weight drives nails and pulls them out. Hold it near the end of the handle and let its weight do the work. Combination pliers grip, bend and cut wire. Long-nosed pliers reach into tight places and hold small parts. An adjustable spanner fits nuts and bolts of many sizes and should be set tight on the nut so that it does not slip and round off the corners.
Measuring and marking

A steel tape measure of five metres or more is essential. The hook on its end is deliberately loose. It slides by exactly its own thickness so that measurements are accurate whether you hook it over an edge or push it against a surface. A spirit level tells you whether something is truly horizontal or vertical. Add a pencil and a square for marking right angles. The old rule is to measure twice and cut once.
Cutting

A utility knife with replaceable blades cuts cardboard, carpet, plasterboard and much else. Change the blade as soon as it dulls, since a blunt blade needs more force and is more likely to slip. Always cut away from your body and retract the blade when you put it down. A small hand saw handles occasional cuts in timber. A junior hacksaw cuts metal and plastic pipe.
The cordless drill

The one power tool worth buying first is a cordless drill that also drives screws. It makes holes in wood, metal and, with the right bit, light masonry, and it saves a great deal of effort when assembling furniture or fixing things to walls. It has an adjustable clutch, a numbered ring behind the chuck, that stops turning at a set resistance so that you do not overdrive screws. Buy a mixed set of drill and driver bits with it.
The small extras

A set of hex keys fits the bolts in flat-pack furniture and many bicycles. A torch, or better a head torch, leaves both hands free under a sink. A roll of strong tape, some cable ties, a selection of screws and wall plugs and a tube of general-purpose glue solve a surprising number of problems. Light machine oil eases stiff hinges and locks. Penetrating spray helps free seized bolts but is not a lasting lubricant.
Safety and quality

Eye protection is cheap and should be worn whenever drilling, hammering or cutting, since fragments travel fast. Gloves help with rough materials. Turn off the power at the breaker before any electrical work and the water at the valve before any plumbing. As for quality, the cheapest tools often fit poorly and wear out quickly. Mid-range tools from an established maker, bought once, will usually last a lifetime of domestic use.
Know what you want to say

Most muddled writing comes from starting before the writer knows the point. A useful test is to state your message aloud in two sentences to someone who knows nothing about it. If you cannot, the difficulty is not with the prose, and no amount of polishing will cure it. Work out the point first. Much of the labour of writing is discovering what you think, and a first draft is often the place where that happens.
Put the point first

Readers are busy and many stop early. State the conclusion at the beginning, then support it. An email should give its request or its news in the first line. A report should open with what was found and what is recommended. School essays teach people to build toward a conclusion. For nearly every practical purpose the reverse order is better. A reader who stops after one paragraph should still leave with the main message.
Short words, short sentences

Use the plain word when it will serve. Use, not utilize. Start, not commence. Help, not facilitate. Long words chosen to impress make a reader work harder and trust the writer less. Keep most sentences to one idea. If a sentence runs beyond two lines, look for the place where it can be split. Vary the lengths so the rhythm does not become monotonous, but let the short, direct sentence be your default.
Prefer the active voice

In an active sentence, the subject acts: the committee rejected the proposal. In a passive one, the subject is acted upon: the proposal was rejected. The passive is longer and often hides who did what, which is why it is so common in official apologies. It has legitimate uses, when the actor is unknown or unimportant. As a habit, name who did the thing and what they did. Your sentences will be shorter and clearer.
Cut

Nearly every draft is improved by removing a tenth of it. Look for words that add nothing: very, really, quite, in order to, the fact that, it should be noted that. Look for sentences that repeat the previous one in different words. Look for an opening paragraph that merely clears the throat. George Orwell, in a well-known essay on English prose, advised cutting any word that can be cut. Readers never complain that something was too easy to read.
The curse of knowledge

Once you understand something, it is hard to remember not understanding it. In a much-cited experiment, people tapped out the rhythm of a familiar song and predicted that listeners would name it about half the time. Listeners managed it on roughly one attempt in forty. The tappers could hear the melody in their heads. Writers are in the same position. Terms and steps that seem obvious to you may be opaque to a reader.
Be concrete

Abstract statements slide past the reader. Examples stay. Sales rose sharply is weaker than sales rose from 200 to 340 units a month. The policy caused problems is weaker than the policy left three branches without a manager for six weeks. Whenever you make a general claim, follow it with a particular case, a number or a name. If you cannot think of one, consider whether the general claim is true.
Read it aloud

The best single editing technique is to read the draft aloud, or have software read it to you. The ear catches what the eye forgives: the sentence that runs out of breath, the word repeated three times, the phrase that sounds pompous, the step missing from an argument. Wherever you stumble, a reader will too. Leave a draft overnight if you can. In the morning you will read it more nearly as a stranger would.
The mistake of putting someone on a hand

Beginners decide that an opponent has ace king and then play the rest of the hand as if that were known. Sometimes they are right, which reinforces the habit. More often the opponent turns over something else and the beginner is baffled. Nobody can deduce two exact cards from a few bets. What can be deduced is the collection of hands consistent with what the opponent has done. That collection is called a range.
Start before the flop

A range begins with the first action. A tight player raising from early position might hold big pairs, ace king, ace queen and a few suited big cards, perhaps one hand in eight. A loose player raising on the button might hold four hands in ten. A player who just calls a raise rarely has aces or kings, since most players reraise those. Position, the action and what you know of the player set the starting list.
Narrow with each action

Every later decision removes hands from the list. Suppose the flop is king, eight, three and the raiser bets. That keeps most of the range, since many players bet any two cards here. The turn is a two and they bet again, larger. Now the weakest hands drop out. On the river they bet a third time. By this point, a typical player's range is mostly a king with a good kicker or better, plus an occasional busted bluff.
Weigh, do not eliminate

Ranges are not just in or out. Some hands are more likely than others within the range. A player might bet three streets with ace king every time and with a bluff one time in five. Good hand readers weight the possibilities instead of crossing them off. They also keep unlikely hands in mind for players who have shown they are capable of odd plays. The picture is a set of probabilities that shifts with each bet.
Your own range

The idea applies to you as well. Your opponents, if they are thinking, are assigning you a range. So ask what your line looks like from across the table. If you would only play a hand this way with very strong holdings, your bets will get too many folds, or your checks will invite bluffs. Thinking about your whole range in a spot, not just the hand you happen to hold, is how good players stay hard to read.
Capped and uncapped

A range is capped when it cannot contain the strongest hands. If a player just calls before the flop and then calls bets on a board of ace, king, queen, they are unlikely to hold a set or two pair of the top cards, having not raised at any point. Their range has a ceiling. A capped range is vulnerable to large bets, because its owner can never be confident. Recognizing when an opponent is capped is a signal to apply pressure.
Compare equity against the range

Once you have a range in mind, the decision is arithmetic. How does your hand do against all of it? If the pot is offering 3 to 1 and your hand beats a third of the hands in their range, call. This is far more reliable than fearing the single worst possibility or hoping for the best one. Software lets you practise this away from the table by entering a range and seeing your equity against it.
Building the habit

Start small. On every hand you watch, even those you have folded, guess the raiser's range before the flop and revise it as the action unfolds. When cards are shown, check whether the hand was inside your range. If it was not, ask what you missed. Over a few months, this turns hand reading from a mysterious talent into a routine, and it works equally well against players you have never seen before.
What a bubble is

A bubble is a sharp rise in the price of an asset that is driven by the expectation of further rises, not by what the asset earns or is used for. People buy because prices are going up, and their buying pushes prices up further. The process sustains itself until new buyers run out. Then prices fall, usually much faster than they rose. Bubbles are easy to identify afterwards and notoriously hard to call at the time.
Tulips

The earliest famous example is from the Dutch Republic in the 1630s. Rare tulip bulbs, especially those with striped petals, became luxury goods, and contracts to buy them changed hands at soaring prices. At the peak, a single prized bulb was reported to cost as much as a fine house. In February 1637 buyers failed to appear at an auction, and the market collapsed within days. Modern historians think the wider economic harm was small and that later moralists exaggerated the tale.
The South Sea

In 1720 the South Sea Company, which held a British trading monopoly of little practical value, offered to take over much of the national debt in exchange for shares. Its share price rose roughly eightfold in a few months, helped by bribes and by lending investors the money to buy. Dozens of imitation companies were floated. By the autumn, the price had collapsed.
